point_one.role: Show why some organizations are moving back toward assigned seats by reframing the seat as an employee-experience tool, not merely a piece of office furniture. The key design insight is a selective hybrid: Gensler’s proposal favors dedicated desks for employees who come in three or more days a week, rather than restoring fixed seating for everyone.
point_one.new_listener_takeaway: The emerging alternative is not simply “assigned seating versus hot-desking,” but attendance- and task-based allocation: frequent office users may need continuity for focus and belonging, while less frequent users can remain flexible. This explains why Amazon’s policy was a restoration in some major U.S. hubs, not a company-wide rejection of hot-desking.
point_one.evidence_anchor: F-01 documents Amazon’s selective restoration and its exclusion of offices that already used hot-desking; F-02 describes Scotiabank’s “quiet shift”; F-03 links fixed seating with higher reported support for focused work—80% versus 67%—and recommends dedicated desks for employees in the office at least three days a week.
point_one.why_it_matters: Listeners can judge a seating-policy reversal more accurately: it may be a targeted attempt to protect concentration, culture, and attachment among regular office users, rather than evidence that flexible seating has failed everywhere. That distinction points toward more practical workplace policies than a universal return to either model.
point_one.must_not_overlap_with_full_story: Do not repeat the headline-level claim that Amazon, Scotiabank, or Gensler represent a return of fixed desks, or simply restate that employees value focus and belonging. The Point should develop the specific attendance-based, mixed-policy solution instead.
point_one.must_not_overlap_with_other_point: Do not explain the industry-wide CBRE and Gartner trend, portfolio efficiency, or the difference between aggregate adoption data and employee experience; those belong to Point Two.

point_two.role: Decode the apparent contradiction by showing that industry statistics and employee-centered evidence are counting different things: portfolio-level seating strategies and future plans on one side, versus the quality of the daily work experience on the other. Add the crucial finding that shared seating is not automatically inferior when it comes with enough workspace variety.
point_two.new_listener_takeaway: A rise in desk sharing does not necessarily mean a clean ideological victory for flexibility or that workers prefer unassigned desks; it can reflect real-estate optimization, while the experience depends on the surrounding design. Make Work Better’s data shows that varied hot-desking environments reached an Lmi of 72.8, above both fixed desks at 69.6 and hot-desking overall at 68.2.
point_two.evidence_anchor: F-06 shows assigned seating falling from 83% to 55% while desk-sharing models rose from 12% to 36%; F-07 records planned expansion of shared desks; F-08 shows the conditional advantage of workspace variety; F-09 illustrates how nominally flexible systems can become informally fixed, with 36.8% reporting that seats tend to become fixed.
point_two.why_it_matters: Listeners gain a better test for workplace claims: ask whether a statistic measures adoption, planned capacity, actual use, or satisfaction, and ask what design supports the seating model. This prevents the industry’s desk-sharing growth from being mistaken for proof that employees experience all hot-desking arrangements as flexible or effective.
point_two.must_not_overlap_with_full_story: Do not repeat the basic CBRE/Gartner numbers merely to prove that desk sharing is expanding, nor restate the article’s central “two trends coexist” conclusion. The Point must interpret what those measurements do—and do not—tell us about the workplace.
point_two.must_not_overlap_with_other_point: Do not focus on why frequent employees want personal continuity, concentration, or belonging, or propose attendance-based assigned seating. Those employee-experience reasons and the mixed-policy remedy belong to Point One.

- new_listener_takeaway: 聞き手がこのPointを聞いて新しく持ち帰る、具体的な
  理解・示唆・視点(Full Storyを聞いただけでは得られないもの)
- evidence_anchor: このPointの内容が、Verified Fact Ledgerのどの事実・
  データに基づくか
- why_it_matters: このPointが「だから何なのか」に対して与える具体的な答え
  (単なる一般的な留保・免責事項ではなく、聞き手にとっての意味)
- must_not_overlap_with_full_story: Full Storyで既に説明される意味のうち、
  このPointで繰り返してはいけない具体的な内容
- must_not_overlap_with_other_point: もう一方のPointが担う内容のうち、
  このPointで重複させてはいけない具体的な内容

【禁止(重要)】
以下のようなPointは、たとえPoint OneとPoint Twoの文字列が違っていても
価値が無いとみなされます。計画段階でこれらを避けてください:
- 研究上の限界・一般化上の注意・免責事項だけで構成されるPoint
- Full Storyの要約・言い換えに留まるPoint
- もう一方のPointの要約・言い換えになっているPoint
- 「だから何なのか」を説明できないPoint
- 他のどんな記事にもほぼそのまま流用できる一般論
- 新しい理解・解釈・意外性・具体的示唆のいずれも加えていないPoint

必要な留保・注意書き自体を書くこと自体は禁止されていませんが、それだけで
Point枠全体を使わないでください(留保は、新しい価値を含む内容に添える
補足として書いてください)。

【出力】
point_one/point_twoそれぞれについて、上記6項目を1〜2文の英語で簡潔に
記述してください(内部設計用であり、リスナーには見せません)。
